docs.text: reality64 ¶ reality64 is a Rust library for running N64 software on PC and other systems. It provides a faithful libultra runtime alongside a modern renderer, audio, and input, so a decompilation runs on its original threading and main.c with minimal change. Features Provided ¶ [x] Libultra runtime (ultra) — real threads, message queues + events, a 60 Hz VI clock, an RCP task engine (graphics → ultragfx, audio → the Rust classic US aspMain handler), PI/DMA, timers, and EEPROM save, all over native pointers [x] Window Management (gui) [x] N64 RDP command processing and rendering via ultragfx on wgpu (gui) [x] Input Handling (gamepad) [x] Audio Rendering via arie (audio) Optional Features ¶ [x] Speech Synthesis (speech) [x] TCP Stream (network) For details on each of the features provided please see our documentation . How to setup? ¶ For setup and more in-depth information please see our documentation . For display-list fixtures and continuous recordings, see ultragfx capture . Community ¶

docs.text: reality64 audio: the libultra AI adapter over Arie ¶ This document defines the boundary between Arie (a general host audio library) and reality64 (a general libultra runtime for N64 PC ports), and the contract the reality64 AI adapter presents to a guest decomp (SM64 today; OOT/MM as future targets). Layering — who owns what ¶ guest decomp (sm64 / oot / …) libultra AI API: osAiSetFrequency, │ osAiSetNextBuffer / osAiGetLength / osAiSetNextBuffer, osAiGetLength, │ osAiGetStatus / osAiSetFrequency osAiGetStatus (unchanged guest code) ▼ reality64 libultra AI shim ── cpp/libultra/os_ai.c + src/audio.rs (AudioRuntime) │ N64 AI semantics and host feeding policy live here ▼ (Arie's Rust API only — never its C ABI) Arie 0.3 ── a general push/queue host-audio library PCM in → resampled → played smoothly; reports occupancy + starvation. Contains no N64/libultra concepts. Reusable by any emulator or port. Arie stays general. Its job is only: accept interleaved PCM at some source rate, resample to the device, play it smoothly, and report queue depth / starvation. An emulator for a different console reuses Arie unchanged and writes its own thin adapter. reality64’s only Arie-side change is a near-prime resampler fix ( resample_ratio_terms ), which is itself a generality improvement — arbitrary source rates (the N64 AI realizes near-prime rates like 32006 Hz) now resample. reality64 owns the N64 feeding policy. The AI’s clock realization, the DMA validation, and — crucially — the buffering policy that keeps Arie fed all live in the reality64 shim, parameterized only by the guest’s realized rate and one knob ( AI_TARGET_DEPTH_MS ). No game-specific constant appears in os_ai.c / audio.rs . The C boundary — six R64Audio* calls ¶ os_ai.c is the only caller of the six extern "C" entry points in audio.rs ; each locks one process-global Mutex<AudioRuntime> (panic-contained via catch_unwind ) and defers to a private method. Only fixed-width scalars cross; no Arie type or header leaks into C ( internal.h never includes <arie/arie.h> ). libultra call reality64 extern behavior osAiSetFrequency R64AudioSetSourceRate realize rate (divisor rule + TV family), install/replace the Arie player; propagate install failure as -1 osAiSetNextBuffer R64AudioSubmit validate the DMA, free-push into Arie osAiGetLength R64AudioCurrentLength faithful current-DMA-remaining bytes osAiGetStatus R64AudioStatus AI_STATUS_FIFO_FULL / AI_STATUS_DMA_BUSY (teardown) R64AudioClear / R64AudioTeardown reset / drop the player The feeding policy (why it is shaped this way) ¶ The N64 AI driver paces itself off osAiGetLength and keeps ~1 video frame (~18 ms) of buffer — correct for hardware, whose DAC drains sample-accurately. A host pipeline (CPAL callback granularity + resampler, badly amplified over Bluetooth) needs a deep, continuously-replenished buffer (~40–80 ms) or it underruns. Three design choices reconcile this without lying to the guest: Free-push submit. osAiSetNextBuffer pushes straight into Arie; Arie’s own software queue is the buffer and its QueueFull is the only backpressure. reality64 keeps no admission FIFO of its own. The earlier hardware-faithful 2-deep FIFO wedged permanently on any starve: Arie’s retired position froze, the FIFO filled, and no fresh audio could be admitted to un-starve it. The non-gating tracker (below) exists purely for reporting and never gates. Deep buffer in Arie’s device ring. AI_TARGET_DEPTH_MS (80 ms) sizes Arie’s prebuffer; the ring is built during prebuffer and refilled at real time. The source queue stays shallow (~2 DMAs); the depth lives in the ring. The software-queue capacity is sized per rate to admit any single legal DMA ( 0x3fff8 bytes) plus one target depth — a ceiling, not a latency target. Faithful osAiGetLength . Reported as bytes remaining in the current DMA only (≤ one DMA), from a non-gating descriptor tracker reaped by Arie’s retired position. The guest paces exactly as on hardware; the host depth is supplied by the prebuffer, not by lying about the queue length. Two host-functional deviations ¶ Where strict hardware fidelity would break host playback, reality64 chooses host-functional behavior and documents it: osAiGetLength is conservative, ~one resampler block late. Arie retires a source block only once the next block’s output has played (the retire watermark), so the reported “current DMA remaining” lags true playback by up to one input chunk. Bounded by the resampler chunk; absorbed by the prebuffer. osAiGetStatus ’s FIFO_FULL is running-and-target-depth, not a 2-deep FIFO. It is set only once Arie is actually Running and total host occupancy ≥ AI_TARGET_DEPTH_MS . Two reasons: (a) target-depth rather than a shallow 2-deep gate, so a status-paced guest builds and holds the deep host buffer instead of starving Arie; (b) the Running requirement — while Arie is still Prebuffering , FIFO_FULL stays clear so the guest keeps feeding until Arie’s own startup low-water (whole resampler blocks producing the device low-water) is met. A target-depth- only gate would latch full below Arie’s effective startup need and deadlock a status-paced guest. osAiGetStatus ’s DMA_BUSY = an accepted, unretired DMA exists. It is set whenever occupancy > 0 — true during Prebuffering and Starved , not gated on the host callback playing — matching the N64 register’s “a DMA is still in flight” meaning; only the terminal backend states ( DeviceLost , CounterExhausted ) clear it. OOT / MM readiness ¶ The adapter is game-agnostic : it implements the standard libultra AI calls with no SM64-specific values, so any decomp that drives audio through them should work unchanged. Two caveats, validated only against SM64 (length-paced) so far: The osAiGetStatus FIFO_FULL = target-depth choice is validated against a length-paced guest (SM64 uses osAiGetLength , not status). A guest that paces submission purely on AI_STATUS_FIFO_FULL is handled by design but unverified. When OOT/MM sources are pinned in-tree, inspect every osAiGetLength / osAiGetStatus call site and add a per-driver trace-compatibility test. Known limitation (outside the validated SM64 profile) ¶ The software queue is sized to admit any single legal AI DMA in frames , but Arie independently caps the number of queued source chunks ( MAXIMUM_SOURCE_CHUNKS = 4096 ). Those 4096 chunks hold only 8192 source frames when each DMA is the minimum legal 2 frames — below the per-rate frame capacity at every supported rate, not just at the high end. So a guest that submits thousands of very small (sub-frame-target) DMAs faster than Arie’s worker drains them into chunks could hit the chunk cap and see a spurious QueueFull before the frame capacity is reached. This is not exercised by SM64, which submits video-frame-sized DMAs (hundreds of frames) at ~16–48 kHz — so the frame-capacity guarantee holds for the validated SM64 profile. It has not been audited for OOT/MM. If a future guest submits many tiny DMAs, eliminate the bound by coalescing adjacent submissions in the shim or raising Arie’s chunk cap; until then this is a documented limitation of the “general” claim, not a proven-universal guarantee. Validation ¶ Correctness of the tracker, free-push, faithful length, osAiGetStatus , and queue sizing is unit-tested (reality64 cargo test --lib audio , ctest reality64_os_ai ). A deterministic-ish sim of the real Arie pipeline ( arie pipeline.rs , run_faithful_sim ) is a rough sanity check, not proof — it is non-deterministic (worker thread + timing) and single-phase. The authoritative gate is the in-game listen test on real Bluetooth hardware , where audio must start and sustain across intro / file-select / in-level with no deadlock or dropout.

docs.text: Audio microcode ¶ reality64 runs a game’s audio command lists itself instead of emulating the RSP. Each handler is written for one microcode revision and reproduces it exactly: the same output samples, the same state in memory, the same DMEM contents after every task. Selector Microcode Data section R64_RSP_AUDIO_ACMD (5) classic aspMain , Super Mario 64 (US) 704 bytes, SHA-256 79bb2a3e8555019bc4b229f0c218f1e329ca5711bfa55c7c7f992facf2e12c83 What the port provides ¶ Register the microcode’s text address with R64RspRegister , as for graphics. Link the real aspMain data section and point OSTask.t.ucode_data at it, with ucode_data_size set to its length. The handler reads its tables from there, the way the RSP loads them at the start of each task, so reality64 itself contains no microcode. Generate the data at build time from the game’s own sources or ROM; don’t commit it. A missing or different data section aborts with a message naming the revision reality64 expected. Commands are reality64’s native Acmd packets: two 64-bit words, with full host pointers wherever the console command carries an RDRAM address. Keep data in the representation the game’s CPU code already uses: PCM, codebooks, loop history and voice state as host-order 16-bit values, compressed ADPCM bytes as they come from the ROM. Keep every audio buffer at the same alignment modulo 8 it had on the console. Like the RSP’s DMA, the handler rounds addresses down to a multiple of 8 and lengths up, so allocations must also cover those rounded extents. Tasks run synchronously on the calling guest thread and keep their state between tasks. A loop or state buffer the game hands to one task must stay alive while later tasks can use it. How it was checked ¶ The handlers were checked against the microcode itself, running on a real N64 and in an interpreter that matches the console byte for byte. Synthetic tasks cover every command’s boundaries; real command lists captured from the game cover ordinary play. Byte-level operations at odd addresses on 16-bit data are the one place the native representation can differ from the console, and no game we know of issues them.

docs.text: ultragfx capture ¶ Set capture variables before launching the game. reality64 must be built against an ultragfx revision with CaptureSequence and the native capture API. The dependency enables ultragfx’s capture feature. A statically linked game must be relinked after rebuilding reality64. Captures use the .ugfxcap extension and ultragfx’s UGFXCAP\0 magic. Use the matching ultragfx replay tool; captures with the old magic are not compatible. Variable Meaning ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_DIR Directory for individual frame fixtures. Requires ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_FRAMES . ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_FRAMES Comma-separated renderer serials for individual fixtures, starting at 1. ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SEQUENCE Output file for one sequence, for example /tmp/startup.ugfxcap . Mutually exclusive with ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_DIR . ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_WARMUP_FRAMES Number of initial sequence frames before observation; defaults to 0. These frames remain in the recording. ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_PRESENTATIONS Required sequence presentation serials, comma-separated, all greater than the warm-up count. ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_REVISION Decomp revision in each frame’s provenance; defaults to unknown . ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SYMBOLS Source symbols or scene annotations in provenance; defaults to unknown (live task) . Lists accept surrounding whitespace, duplicate serials, and empty comma-separated elements, including the trailing comma produced by BSD seq -s, . Empty lists, zero, invalid numbers, and invalid combinations cause render-thread failure and runtime shutdown. Existing capture files are never overwritten. Auxiliary variables alone do not enable capture. Individual frames ¶ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_DIR = /tmp/sm64-frames \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_FRAMES = 120 ,240,360, \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_REVISION = " $( git rev-parse HEAD ) " \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SYMBOLS = 'live sm64 graphics tasks' \ RUST_LOG = reality64::render = info \ ./build-cmake/sm64-us This writes frame-000120.ugfxcap , frame-000240.ugfxcap , and frame-000360.ugfxcap , named from fixture.frame.serial . Serial 1 is the first graphics task, including startup before gameplay. PR #33 used zero-based consume indices, so its selection 120 wrote serial 121; this hook selects the renderer serial directly. Add one to old selections to capture the same tasks. Standalone fixtures still require self-contained frame state. A frame that depends on prior RDP/TMEM or framebuffer history can fail standalone capture or replay; use a sequence for those workloads. Capture failures log an error and request shutdown. A successful write logs captured frame ... . Sequences ¶ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SEQUENCE = /tmp/sm64-startup.ugfxcap \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_WARMUP_FRAMES = 120 \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_PRESENTATIONS = 121 ,180,240, \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_REVISION = " $( git rev-parse HEAD ) " \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SYMBOLS = 'startup through selected gameplay route' \ RUST_LOG = reality64::render = info \ ./build-cmake/sm64-us The sequence resets the renderer before the first task and records every frame through serial 240. It retains frames 1–120 as warm-up and selects 121, 180, and 240 for replay images. Serials are never cropped or renumbered. Each reality64 graphics task is one frame. The dither seed is 0 and depth reset policy is Never . After serial 240 is presented, CaptureSequence::finish validates the recording, the file is written, and recording stops. The game continues running. Look for capture sequence started: ... frames 1..=240 and capture sequence complete: wrote 240 frames to ... in the log. The completed file uses the version-two sequence container, not a standalone frame payload. Sequence startup also logs capture sequence context initialization #1 with the process ID. A second sequence context in the same process logs its attempt number and fails before creating a renderer or recording. It cannot restart at serial 1 and compete for the same output. reality64’s current GUI starts one render context; resuming an existing window does not recreate it. Restart the process for another sequence, even after the first finishes. Guest memory is copied inside consume_dl , before the blocked guest is released. All sequence renderer operations use the capture wrapper. Presentation uses present_last , without VI registers or guest-memory reads. Renderer resizes are deferred until recording finishes to keep one extent and avoid invalidating the sequence. Avoid resizing or minimizing during a recording: a surface presentation failure stops capture and attempts to save the earlier completed prefix. Without a capture output variable, reality64 retains the normal renderer operations and presentation error handling and installs no signal handler. Ending a run early ¶ Sequence mode attempts to install a ctrlc handler with termination support once per process, including when installation fails. Success logs capture shutdown handler installed . With that handler, Ctrl-C, SIGTERM ( kill -TERM <game-pid> ), SIGHUP, and normal window close reach reality64’s shutdown path, which joins the render thread after it finishes and writes completed frames. Allow shutdown to finish; a second forced kill can interrupt serialization. Failure logs capture shutdown handler unavailable and warns that a killed run will not save an unfinished capture. Recording continues: endpoint and normal window-close saves remain enabled. The sequence-start message alone does not promise signal save. ctrlc::try_set_handler also rejects existing native signal handlers and ignored signals, so its “already registered” error does not prove reality64 initialized twice. Existing signal dispositions are not deliberately overwritten. For a prefix ending at serial N, requested presentations greater than N are removed. If none were reached, N becomes the sole presentation. Warm-up becomes min(requested_warmup, N - 1) . Every frame 1..N remains present. The log says capture sequence incomplete with the actual counts and selection, followed by capture sequence partial: wrote N frames ... . This is a valid partial recording, not evidence that the requested range completed. If no frame completed, there is no valid sequence to write; the error says so. SIGKILL, process abort, power loss, or a render-thread panic cannot reliably save an unfinished recording. CaptureSequence keeps frames in memory and only exposes them through consuming finish ; it has no snapshot/checkpoint API. This hook saves on catchable termination and at the requested endpoint. It does not install unsafe signal handlers or claim crash recovery. Memory grows with the retained prefix, and serialization needs additional memory. Writes use a unique <output>.<pid>-<id>.partial file in the output directory, sync its bytes, then atomically publish the final name with a hard link. The filesystem must support hard links. The final path never exposes a half-written container. Empty staging files are removed on graceful abandonment; crashes can leave them behind without blocking retries. Failed writes/publications can leave nonempty staging files; the error identifies the path. Validate such a file with the replay tool before using it. A .partial file alone is not a successful capture. Replay and validation ¶ From the ultragfx worktree, with its supported toolchain: mkdir -p /tmp/sm64-replay cargo run -p ultragfx --features capture --example replay_capture -- \ /tmp/sm64-startup.ugfxcap /tmp/sm64-replay/startup all The replay loader rejects gaps, missing reset history, invalid warm-up/presentation metadata, and malformed/truncated files. The all mode replays depth policies persist , cimg , task , and frame ; it writes per-policy logs and selected serial PNG/RGBA8 files, plus comparisons against persistence. For example, expect startup-persist-000121.png , startup-persist-000180.png , startup-persist-000240.png , and startup-persist.log . Check that the log lists every original frame 1..240, warm-up 120, the three requested presentations, expected provenance, one native task per frame, and no missing-memory errors. Review the images against the live route. Container validation alone does not establish visual correctness.

Empty lists, zero, invalid numbers, and invalid combinations cause render-thread failure and runtime shutdown. Existing capture files are never overwritten. Auxiliary variables alone do not enable capture.

docs.text: ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_DIR = /tmp/sm64-frames \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_FRAMES = 120 ,240,360, \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_REVISION = " $( git rev-parse HEAD ) " \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SYMBOLS = 'live sm64 graphics tasks' \ RUST_LOG = reality64::render = info \ ./build-cmake/sm64-us This writes frame-000120.ugfxcap , frame-000240.ugfxcap , and frame-000360.ugfxcap , named from fixture.frame.serial . Serial 1 is the first graphics task, including startup before gameplay. PR #33 used zero-based consume indices, so its selection 120 wrote serial 121; this hook selects the renderer serial directly. Add one to old selections to capture the same tasks. Standalone fixtures still require self-contained frame state. A frame that depends on prior RDP/TMEM or framebuffer history can fail standalone capture or replay; use a sequence for those workloads. Capture failures log an error and request shutdown. A successful write logs captured frame ... .
docs.title: Individual frames

docs.text: ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SEQUENCE = /tmp/sm64-startup.ugfxcap \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_WARMUP_FRAMES = 120 \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_PRESENTATIONS = 121 ,180,240, \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_REVISION = " $( git rev-parse HEAD ) " \ ULTRAGFX_CAPTURE_SYMBOLS = 'startup through selected gameplay route' \ RUST_LOG = reality64::render = info \ ./build-cmake/sm64-us The sequence resets the renderer before the first task and records every frame through serial 240. It retains frames 1–120 as warm-up and selects 121, 180, and 240 for replay images. Serials are never cropped or renumbered. Each reality64 graphics task is one frame. The dither seed is 0 and depth reset policy is Never . After serial 240 is presented, CaptureSequence::finish validates the recording, the file is written, and recording stops. The game continues running. Look for capture sequence started: ... frames 1..=240 and capture sequence complete: wrote 240 frames to ... in the log. The completed file uses the version-two sequence container, not a standalone frame payload. Sequence startup also logs capture sequence context initialization #1 with the process ID. A second sequence context in the same process logs its attempt number and fails before creating a renderer or recording. It cannot restart at serial 1 and compete for the same output. reality64’s current GUI starts one render context; resuming an existing window does not recreate it. Restart the process for another sequence, even after the first finishes. Guest memory is copied inside consume_dl , before the blocked guest is released. All sequence renderer operations use the capture wrapper. Presentation uses present_last , without VI registers or guest-memory reads. Renderer resizes are deferred until recording finishes to keep one extent and avoid invalidating the sequence. Avoid resizing or minimizing during a recording: a surface presentation failure stops capture and attempts to save the earlier completed prefix. Without a capture output variable, reality64 retains the normal renderer operations and presentation error handling and installs no signal handler.
docs.title: Sequences

docs.text: Sequence mode attempts to install a ctrlc handler with termination support once per process, including when installation fails. Success logs capture shutdown handler installed . With that handler, Ctrl-C, SIGTERM ( kill -TERM <game-pid> ), SIGHUP, and normal window close reach reality64’s shutdown path, which joins the render thread after it finishes and writes completed frames. Allow shutdown to finish; a second forced kill can interrupt serialization. Failure logs capture shutdown handler unavailable and warns that a killed run will not save an unfinished capture. Recording continues: endpoint and normal window-close saves remain enabled. The sequence-start message alone does not promise signal save. ctrlc::try_set_handler also rejects existing native signal handlers and ignored signals, so its “already registered” error does not prove reality64 initialized twice. Existing signal dispositions are not deliberately overwritten. For a prefix ending at serial N, requested presentations greater than N are removed. If none were reached, N becomes the sole presentation. Warm-up becomes min(requested_warmup, N - 1) . Every frame 1..N remains present. The log says capture sequence incomplete with the actual counts and selection, followed by capture sequence partial: wrote N frames ... . This is a valid partial recording, not evidence that the requested range completed. If no frame completed, there is no valid sequence to write; the error says so. SIGKILL, process abort, power loss, or a render-thread panic cannot reliably save an unfinished recording. CaptureSequence keeps frames in memory and only exposes them through consuming finish ; it has no snapshot/checkpoint API. This hook saves on catchable termination and at the requested endpoint. It does not install unsafe signal handlers or claim crash recovery. Memory grows with the retained prefix, and serialization needs additional memory. Writes use a unique <output>.<pid>-<id>.partial file in the output directory, sync its bytes, then atomically publish the final name with a hard link. The filesystem must support hard links. The final path never exposes a half-written container. Empty staging files are removed on graceful abandonment; crashes can leave them behind without blocking retries. Failed writes/publications can leave nonempty staging files; the error identifies the path. Validate such a file with the replay tool before using it. A .partial file alone is not a successful capture.
docs.title: Ending a run early

docs.text: From the ultragfx worktree, with its supported toolchain: mkdir -p /tmp/sm64-replay cargo run -p ultragfx --features capture --example replay_capture -- \ /tmp/sm64-startup.ugfxcap /tmp/sm64-replay/startup all The replay loader rejects gaps, missing reset history, invalid warm-up/presentation metadata, and malformed/truncated files. The all mode replays depth policies persist , cimg , task , and frame ; it writes per-policy logs and selected serial PNG/RGBA8 files, plus comparisons against persistence. For example, expect startup-persist-000121.png , startup-persist-000180.png , startup-persist-000240.png , and startup-persist.log . Check that the log lists every original frame 1..240, warm-up 120, the three requested presentations, expected provenance, one native task per frame, and no missing-memory errors. Review the images against the live route. Container validation alone does not establish visual correctness.

docs.text: Features ¶ GUI ¶ reality64 provides a GUI library for creating windows and rendering graphics. The GUI library is currently a work in progress and is not yet complete. ImGui / imgui-rs is used for drawing, if you’re working on a C/C++ project, you’ll need to include the ImGui headers to your project: // If C++ #include <imgui/imgui.h> // If C (make sure to set CIMGUI_DEFINE_ENUMS_AND_STRUCTS to 1) #include <cimgui/cimgui.h> The following API is provided: /** * Can be used to get the display's aspect ratio **/ float R64DisplayGetAspectRatio (); Audio ¶ reality64 provides functionality for audio playback. Speech ¶ reality64 provides an API for text-to-speech (TTS): /** * Creates and sets up the audio synthesizer, returning a pointer to the instance or nullptr if creation failed **/ void * SpeechSynthesizerCreate ( void ); // Rust: let mut speech_synthesizer = SpeechSynthesizer::new().unwrap(); /** * Frees the speech synthesizer instance. **/ void SpeechSynthesizerFree ( void * synthesizer ); // Rust: no dedicated method, instance drop will deallocate it /** * Sets the volume for the synthesizer, scale from 0-1. **/ void SpeechSynthesizerSetVolume ( void * synthesizer , float volume ); // Rust: speech_synthesizer.set_volume(volume: f32) /** * Sets the language of the speaker, takes in a en-US type locale. **/ void SpeechSynthesizerSetLanguage ( void * synthesizer , const char * language ); // Rust: speech_synthesizer.set_language(language: &str) /** * Sets the gender of the speaker, accepted values: SpeechSynthesizerGenderFemale/Male/Neutral. **/ void SpeechSynthesizerSetGender ( void * synthesizer , SpeechSynthesizerGender gender ); // Rust: speech_synthesizer.set_gender(gender: SpeechSynthesizerGender) /** * Dictates the given text, specifying whether previous utterances should be interrupted. **/ void SpeechSynthesizerSpeak ( void * synthesizer , const char * text , uint8_t interrupt ); // Rust: speech_synthesizer.speak(text: &str, interrupt: bool)

docs.text: Input replay ¶ REALITY64_INPUT_RECORD=/path/route.input records controller changes at osViSwapBuffer . REALITY64_INPUT_REPLAY=/path/route.input replays them. Both can be set to extend a route with live input after its end. The version 1 format remains unchanged: reality64-input 1 1 0 0000 0 0 10 8000 0 0 12 0000 0 0 end 60 The header’s last number is the connected-controller bit mask. Each change is swap buttons-hex stick-x stick-y ; swaps start at zero. end is inclusive and otherwise defaults to the last change. Input before the first change is neutral. Existing route files need no conversion. During replay, VI advances only when no positive-priority guest thread is ready. Each step advances one NTSC/MPAL or PAL retrace, services guest timers, then posts VI with the registered divisor. The scheduler retains the run token while injecting events and drains runnable guest work before advancing again. Input still changes at swaps, so the retrace that samples a change follows guest progress. osGetTime and osGetCount read this virtual clock; time does not advance while guest code or a synchronous graphics task is running. Timers fire at the first idle retrace at or after their deadline, before that retrace’s VI message. Playback runs as fast as guest work and rendering allow. It is not a measurement of ordinary play’s wall-clock pacing. Busy waits for time without blocking the guest scheduler cannot progress in this mode. VI must be registered before a guest blocks waiting for a timer. After the inclusive end swap, the next swap returns to live input and starts the ordinary VI and timer clocks. Guest time stays continuous and pending timers retain their remaining duration. Recording alone and play without a valid replay keep their ordinary timing. This controls guest VI, timer and input ordering. It is not a general emulator snapshot: start from the same executable, assets and save. Other host-driven services must be controlled separately if a guest uses them. Native OoT’s audio driver is stubbed; its graphics and DMA completions execute under the guest run token. The parity harness also fixes the game’s RNG seed.

docs.text: Integration ¶ C/C++ Project ¶ If you’re working on a C or C++ project the recommended way of integrating reality64 into your project is using CMake. You can easily build and link this library by using Corrosion , a tool that integrate Rust libraries into C/C++ projects. You’ll want to: Add this library as a submodule (or copy it) into your project Enable Corrosion using FetchContent (see their README) Include the features you want to be built using FEATURES . audio is always included. Link against the reality64 library Include the include folder of reality64 so your program can see the available methods Include the cpp folder into your compilation (this is our C++ API wrapper providing a nicer API for the C language) NOTE: If you get a build error that certain header methods are not implemented, you’re likely not building with that feature enabled. Example: corrosion_import_crate ( MANIFEST_PATH $ { CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR } / .. / reality64 / Cargo . toml FEATURES network ) # methods in these headers will work: # include <reality64/network.h> , <reality64/audio.h> # methods in these headers won't work: # include <reality64/speech.h> Advanced Example: #==============================================================================# # reality64 Integration # #==============================================================================# add_subdirectory ( ./corrosion ) corrosion_import_crate ( MANIFEST_PATH ./reality64/Cargo.toml ) target_link_libraries ( sm64. ${ VERSION } PRIVATE reality64 ) target_include_directories ( sm64. ${ VERSION } PRIVATE ./reality64/include ) if ( APPLE ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework OpenGL" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework Foundation" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework CoreFoundation -framework AVFoundation -framework CoreAudio -framework AudioToolbox" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework Metal -framework QuartzCore" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework IOKit" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework ApplicationServices" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-framework AppKit" ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-lc++" ) elseif ( WIN32 ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE OpenGL32 ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE D3DCompiler ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE imm32 ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE winmm ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE uxtheme ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE dwmapi ) if ( MINGW ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE "-lstdc++" ) endif () else () find_package ( X11 REQUIRED ) find_package ( libUsb REQUIRED ) find_package ( ALSA REQUIRED ) find_package ( PulseAudio REQUIRED ) find_package ( Freetype REQUIRED ) find_package ( udev REQUIRED ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE ${ ALSA_LIBRARY } ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE ${ OPENGL_glx_LIBRARY } ${ OPENGL_opengl_LIBRARY } ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE ${ X11_LIBRARIES } ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE ${ UDEV_LIBRARY } ) target_link_libraries ( reality64 INTERFACE docs.text: Native interpolation sidecars ¶ include/reality64/interpolation.h exposes annotation ABI 2. Call R64InterpolationRegister(R64_INTERPOLATION_ABI_VERSION) once at startup. It returns zero on success or -1 with an error diagnostic on an ABI mismatch. Check that result. Initialize R64TaskAnnotations with R64_TASK_ANNOTATIONS_INIT , then set source , epoch , producer_sample , draws and draw_count . Attach it to the graphics OSTask* with R64InterpolationAttach(task, &annotations) before osSpTaskStartGo . Attachment validates and copies the complete sidecar, including matrix bindings, palette parts and billboard recipes. Guest storage may be reused as soon as attachment returns. The task consumes its attachment once; attaching again before consumption fails. Tasks without an attachment retain the empty annotations used by the opt-in path. Sizes and counts use uintptr_t , including on ports whose local size_t remains 32-bit. Versions, enum tags and flags use uint32_t ; identities and timestamps use uint64_t . The header supplies size fields for every variable-length element layout. The caller must provide a readable version/flags/struct_size prefix and readable allocations for every nonempty array. Validation rejects mismatched sizes, null or misaligned arrays, unknown tags, nonfinite recipes and excessive counts. Limits are 16,384 scopes and 65,536 total bindings and palette parts per task, separately. Invalid input returns -1 with a diagnostic. A scope selects the native address of a call or branch command, not its target. has_occurrence = 0 requires that command to execute exactly once. Set it to 1 to select the zero-based occurrence . Static descendants inherit the scope. R64DrawIdentity supplies the cross-source identity. Command and matrix addresses are task-local operands, never persistent object IDs. Policies map directly to Interpolate, StaticWorld, HoldModel, BillboardHold, ScreenSpace and Hold. Bind allocated View/Projection operands, or an opaque ViewProjection operand. The engine resolves each binding at actual matrix reads, including late rewrites. Palette parts map consecutive 64-byte slots to semantic parts. Billboard recipes carry anchor, scale, spin in radians, row-vector basis and CPU or segment-1 provenance. World geometry marked Hold makes an ABI 2 source ineligible. It repeats the whole source endpoint; it does not freeze just that geometry while the camera moves. ScreenSpace is for UI. World pose holds require HoldModel or BillboardHold. producer_sample is an opaque producer timestamp. epoch is the producer’s continuity generation. events and R64_INTERPOLATION_FRAMEBUFFER_DEPENDENT are producer diagnostics reserved by the ABI. The producer must change epoch across a dependency interval and on its exit; the flag itself is not an engine admission reason. Engine framebuffer admission still runs independently. Task cookies and monotonic swap timestamps remain host-owned. Sidecar conversion does not change consume, guest write-back, completion, SP and DP ordering. The default mode is Original. A port can call R64SetRefreshRate(mode, hz) at any point, including from a settings menu. Modes are R64_REFRESH_ORIGINAL , R64_REFRESH_DISPLAY and R64_REFRESH_MANUAL . Pass zero Hz for Original/Display; Manual accepts positive finite Hz. Invalid input returns -1 with a diagnostic and preserves the previous setting. Ports own their defaults and persistence. REALITY64_REFRESH_RATE=original|display|manual:<hz> overrides the port setting for development. Invalid values fail at startup, including during capture. Capture forces Original. The former REALITY64_FRAME_INTERPOLATION variable is obsolete. Settings take effect at the next VI swap. R64InterpolationActive() reports the value latched at the last swap, so ports can avoid building sidecars in Original. The first swap after enabling interpolation presents a plain image; compatible retained tasks from later swaps establish a pair. Registration and annotation ABI 2 are unchanged. Only registered ports retain tasks when interpolation is active. Ultragfx owns the native surface and its present thread. Original acknowledges each presentation before returning. Display and Manual accept immutable scanouts asynchronously, keeping the newest sources. Missing or stale annotations break the pair and still present the real framebuffer. Phases never alter canonical output or guest write-back. The latest task before the swap is selected explicitly; a no-swap task creates no source. Reality64 supplies the current monitor’s nominal millihertz at startup and on moves/resizes. Unknown rates use 60 Hz. Manual retains its requested rate and clamps the effective rate to the display. The scheduler paces before surface acquisition, delays interpolation by the larger of the last two source intervals plus the preparation lead, and rebases on rate changes. It retains the preceding pair until the delayed sample reaches the latest pair. Its phase time is an estimate, not a physical scanout timestamp or a VRR guarantee. Until presenter B merges, this branch patches ultragfx to /Users/ci/hub/wt/fast3d-rs-ultragfx-refresh-rate/ultragfx . Replace that local patch with the merged revision before sharing the branch.

Until presenter B merges, this branch patches ultragfx to /Users/ci/hub/wt/fast3d-rs-ultragfx-refresh-rate/ultragfx . Replace that local patch with the merged revision before sharing the branch.
